content: Dengue viruses are transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito. Symptoms of dengue typically begin within a few days of being bitten, but in some cases, they may take up to two weeks to manifest. The symptoms can range from mild to severe and may include fever accompanied by nausea, vomiting, rash, headache, pain behind the eyes, and joint and muscle pain. In severe cases, dengue can lead to complications such as shock, internal bleeding, and even death. Not everyone infected with dengue will experience symptoms. Only about one in four infected individuals will feel sick. However, the likelihood of developing severe dengue increases if a person has been previously infected with the virus. Infants and pregnant women are also at a higher risk of severe dengue. Mosquitoes that spread dengue are most active during the day, although they can also bite at night. These mosquitoes are commonly found in tropical and subtropical regions, including areas in the Americas, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and the Pacific Islands. Travelers should check if dengue is a concern at their destination, particularly during warmer months when mosquito activity is higher. To prevent dengue, travelers can take several precautions. Using insect repellents registered with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is highly effective and safe, even for pregnant and breastfeeding women, when used as directed. If sunscreen is also being applied, insect repellent should be applied after the sunscreen. For children, additional precautions include dressing them in clothing that covers their arms and legs, covering strollers and baby carriers with mosquito netting, and carefully applying insect repellent. Products containing oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE) or para-menthane-diol (PMD) should not be used on children under three years old. Insect repellent should not be applied to a child’s hands, eyes, mouth, cuts, or irritated skin. Adults should spray repellent onto their hands first before applying it to a child’s face. Permethrin, an insecticide, can be used to treat clothing and gear such as boots, pants, socks, and tents. Alternatively, travelers can purchase pre-treated clothing and gear. Permethrin-treated items remain effective after multiple washes, but it is important to follow product instructions to determine how long the protection lasts. Permethrin should never be applied directly to the skin. To keep mosquitoes out of living spaces, travelers should choose accommodations with air conditioning or window and door screens. If staying in a place without these features or sleeping outdoors, using a mosquito net is essential. Mosquito nets treated with permethrin provide additional protection compared to untreated nets. When purchasing a mosquito net, select one that is compact, white, rectangular, and has 156 holes per square inch. Ensure it is long enough to tuck under the mattress. If bitten by mosquitoes, avoid scratching the bites. Over-the-counter anti-itch or antihistamine creams can be applied to relieve itching. Currently, there are no dengue vaccine recommendations for travelers.
